title: Abel-Ruffini Theorem
description: A pedagogical walkthrough of the Abel-Ruffini theorem (Wiedijk #16) composed from Mathlib's Galois theory infrastructure: the contrapositive chain from solvability by radicals (`IsSolvableByRad`) through solvable Galois groups (`IsSolvable q.Gal`) to the non-solvability of S₅ (since A₅ is simple and non-abelian), organized as 9 theorems across 187 lines with zero sorries and zero axioms. There is no general solution in radicals to polynomial equations of degree five or higher — first proved by Abel (1824) and later illuminated by Galois's theory connecting radical solvability to group structure.

overview.historicalContext:
The quest to solve polynomial equations drove mathematics for centuries. Quadratic equations were solved in antiquity, cubic equations by Cardano (1545), and quartic equations by Ferrari (1545). For 300 years, mathematicians sought a quintic formula. Joseph-Louis Lagrange's 1770 *Réflexions sur la résolution algébrique des équations* was the crucial precursor: he analyzed why the classical formulas for degrees 2–4 worked by studying permutations of roots ('resolvents'), and noticed that his method broke down for degree 5 — the resolvent of a quintic had degree 6, not lower.

In parallel, Alexandre-Théophile Vandermonde's *Mémoire sur la résolution des équations* (presented to the Académie in 1770, published in 1771) developed similar resolvent ideas independently and applied them with striking success to the cyclotomic equation $x^{11} - 1 = 0$, exhibiting an explicit radical formula for the eleventh roots of unity. Vandermonde's calculation — which today is recognized as a discrete Fourier transform over $\mathbb{Z}/11\mathbb{Z}$ — was the first concrete example of a polynomial of degree above 4 being solved by radicals via group-theoretic considerations. It directly anticipated Gauss's 1801 *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* §VII, where the constructibility of the regular 17-gon was reduced to solving $x^{17} - 1 = 0$ by radicals via the cyclic structure of $(\mathbb{Z}/17\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$. Together, Lagrange and Vandermonde isolated the two facts whose tension Galois would resolve fifty years later: resolvents work when the symmetry group has a nice composition series (Vandermonde's success on cyclotomy), and resolvents fail when it does not (Lagrange's degree-6 obstruction for the quintic).

Paolo Ruffini gave an incomplete proof in 1799 that no such formula exists. His 516-page *Teoria generale delle equazioni* attempted to show that no rational function of the roots could serve as a resolvent, but the proof had gaps — notably an incomplete treatment of permutation groups (the concept barely existed). Augustin-Louis Cauchy, who proved key results on permutation groups in 1815 (including that a primitive subgroup of $S_p$ containing a $p$-cycle equals $S_p$), acknowledged Ruffini's priority but did not endorse the proof.

Niels Henrik Abel provided the first rigorous proof in 1824, at age 21. Living in poverty in Norway, Abel could not afford journal publication and self-published a six-page pamphlet (*Mémoire sur les équations algébriques*), compressed to save printing costs, which he sent to leading mathematicians — Gauss reportedly never read it. Abel refined the argument in an 1826 *Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik* paper. He died of tuberculosis in 1829 at age 26, two days before a letter arrived offering him a professorship in Berlin.

But it was Évariste Galois who revealed the deeper truth: the solvability of a polynomial is determined by the structure of its symmetry group. His theory explains not just why quintics are unsolvable, but precisely which polynomials can be solved by radicals. Galois submitted his work three times to the Académie des Sciences — Cauchy reviewed the first manuscript (1829) but it was never officially reported, Fourier was sent the second (February 1830) but died in May 1830 before completing his review and the manuscript was lost, and Poisson rejected the third (January 1831) as 'incomprehensible.' Tragically killed in a duel at age 20 in 1832, Galois spent the night before writing a letter to Auguste Chevalier summarizing his theory, with marginal notes including the famous 'je n'ai pas le temps' ('I have not the time').

Galois's manuscripts were finally published by Joseph Liouville in 1846, fourteen years after his death. It took another generation — through the work of Camille Jordan (*Traité des substitutions*, 1870) and others — for the full power of Galois theory to be understood. Today it is fundamental to modern algebra, connecting field extensions to group theory and underpinning algebraic number theory, algebraic geometry, and the Langlands program.

**Extended context (companion gallery entries).** This theorem heads a long methodological lineage, each strand cross-linked below: Wantzel's 1837 compass-and-straightedge impossibilities (`angle-trisection`); Hilbert's Satz 90 and Kummer theory turning cyclic Galois actions into radicals; the Burnside $p^aq^b$ and Feit-Thompson odd-order theorems pinning $A_5$ as the minimal non-solvable group (`abel-ruffini-galois-extensions-oq-07`); Eisenstein irreducibility producing the witness $x^5-4x+2$ (`abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01`); the Tschirnhaus-Bring-Klein normal forms and Hermite's 1858 elliptic-modular quintic solution as the positive complement (`abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-07`); the Arnold-Khovanskii topological proof; and Bhargava's 2023 resolution of van der Waerden's genericity conjecture. Previously inlined as standalone key-insight essays, these are kept here in digest form and developed in full in the linked entries.
overview.problemStatement:
Theorem (Abel-Ruffini): There is no general solution in radicals to polynomial equations of degree five or higher.

More precisely: there exist polynomials of degree 5 (and higher) whose roots cannot be expressed using only addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and nth roots applied to the coefficients.

Galois's formulation: A polynomial equation is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is a solvable group.

The symmetric group $S_5$ is not solvable (because the alternating group $A_5$ is simple and non-abelian), so the general quintic, which has Galois group $S_5$, cannot be solved by radicals.

overview.proofStrategy:
The proof connects two seemingly unrelated concepts through Galois's fundamental insight:

1. **FIELD EXTENSIONS**: An element $\alpha \in E$ is *solvable by radicals* over $F$ if it lies in a tower $F = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots \subset K_m \ni \alpha$ where each $K_{i+1} = K_i(\sqrt[n_i]{a_i})$. Mathlib formalizes this as `IsSolvableByRad F α`.

2. **GALOIS GROUPS**: For a polynomial $q(x) \in F[x]$, its Galois group $\text{Gal}(q) \leq S_n$ captures the symmetries of its roots — the automorphisms of the splitting field that fix $F$. Lean represents this as `q.Gal : Type*`.

3. **THE BRIDGE** (`galois_bridge`): $\alpha \in \text{solvableByRad}(F, E) \Rightarrow \text{IsSolvable}(\text{Gal}(\text{minpoly}_F(\alpha)))$. Each radical step $K_i \to K_{i+1} = K_i(\sqrt[n]{a})$ yields a cyclic (hence abelian) Galois group quotient; a group built from abelian quotients is solvable.

4. **GROUP THEORY**: A group $G$ is solvable iff its derived series $G \supset [G,G] \supset [[G,G],[G,G]] \supset \cdots$ reaches $\{e\}$. Crucially:
   - $S_2, S_3, S_4$ are solvable (explaining why quadratics, cubics, quartics have radical formulas)
   - $S_5$ is NOT solvable: $D^1(S_5) = A_5$ and $D^k(S_5) = A_5$ for all $k \geq 1$, because $A_5$ is perfect ($[A_5, A_5] = A_5$, a consequence of its simplicity)

5. **CONCLUSION** (`not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`): By contrapositive of the bridge, $\neg\,\text{IsSolvable}(\text{Gal}(q)) \Rightarrow \neg\,\text{IsSolvableByRad}\,F\,\alpha$. Since $S_5$ is not solvable and the generic quintic has Galois group $S_5$, the general quintic cannot be solved by radicals. The Lean proof is a 2-line `intro`/`exact`.
keyInsights: **The Galois Bridge:** `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` captures: $\alpha$ solvable by radicals over $F$ $\Rightarrow$ $\text{Gal}(\text{minpoly}(\alpha))$ solvable. The contrapositive (used in `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`) gives the impossibility: $\text{Gal}(q)$ not solvable $\Rightarrow$ roots of $q$ not solvable by radicals.

**Degree 5 Threshold via Derived Series:** $S_4$ has derived length 3: $D^1(S_4) = A_4$, $D^2(S_4) = V_4$, $D^3(S_4) = \{e\}$ (since $V_4$ is abelian). A composition series (refining the derived series) is $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \langle(12)(34)\rangle \supset \{e\}$ with cyclic prime-order quotients. Contrast with $S_5$: $D^k(S_5) = A_5$ for all $k \geq 1$ (stuck — $A_5$ is perfect: $[A_5,A_5] = A_5$). This is why degree 4 has a radical formula but degree 5 does not.

**A₅ is the Key Obstruction:** $|A_5| = 60$, $A_5$ is the smallest non-abelian simple group. `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five` formalizes this. The Klein four-group $V_4 = \{e,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$ makes $A_4$ solvable; no analog exists in $A_5$.

**Ferrari's Resolvent Cubic as $S_4 / V_4 \cong S_3$: The Concrete Bridge from Classical Formula to Galois Theory.** Ferrari's 1545 quartic formula reduces the quartic $x^4 + px^2 + qx + r$ to a *resolvent cubic* — a cubic equation in an auxiliary variable whose roots, once known, complete the quartic by two further square-root extractions.

**Mathlib Integration Pattern — Four Modules Compose Into Nine Wrappers:** The 187-line file delegates the entire mathematical content of Abel-Ruffini to four Mathlib modules, then exposes nine theorem-shaped views onto that content with proofs that average under two lines.

**S_n Unsolvability for n ≥ 5:** `symmetric_group_not_solvable` proves $\forall n \geq 5$, $S_n$ not solvable, using `Cardinal.mk (Fin n) ≥ 5` via `simp`. Instances for $S_0, S_1$ (`inferInstance`) vs the impossibility for $S_5, S_6, \ldots$ illustrate the sharp boundary.

**Original Contributions Are Wrappers — The Three-Delegation Pedagogical Architecture:** The file's three original theorems all reduce to a single `exact` or one-line tactic call on a Mathlib lemma. (i) `galois_bridge` (lines 64–67, **2-line body**) delegates directly: `solvableByRad.isSolvable' hq hroot hrad`.

**Transitive Subgroups of $S_5$: The Five Possible Galois Groups for an Irreducible Quintic.** For any irreducible $f \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$ of degree 5, $\text{Gal}(f/\mathbb{Q})$ acts faithfully and transitively on the 5 roots (irreducibility is equivalent to transitivity), hence embeds as a transitive subgroup of $S_5$.

**Jordan-Hölder Guarantees Completeness:** The analysis of $S_n$ via the derived series (keyInsight #2) is not ad hoc — the *Jordan-Hölder theorem* (Jordan 1869, Hölder 1889) guarantees that any two composition series of a finite group $G$ have the same multiset of composition factors up to isomorphism and reordering.

**Kummer Theory Powers Each Radical Step:** Why is each radical extension's Galois group cyclic in the first place? Kummer theory (developed in the 1840s for cyclotomic fields, generalized by Helmut Hasse in the 1920s and reformulated cohomologically by Tate): for a field $K$ containing a primitive $n$th root of unity (with $\text{char}(K) \nmid n$), the cyclic Galois extensions of $K$ with exponent dividing $n$ correspond bijectively to subgroups of $K^*/(K^*)^n$.

conclusion.summary:
This formalization is Wiedijk theorem #16 — one of the 100 landmark mathematical results tracked for formal proof. It demonstrates one of mathematics' most beautiful connections: the solution of polynomial equations reduces to group theory. Galois's insight that symmetry groups control solvability unified algebra in a profound way, transforming a 300-year search for a quintic formula into a structural impossibility with a clean mathematical explanation.

The Lean formalization in 187 lines (zero sorries, zero axioms) works as a pedagogical walkthrough: the three original theorems (`galois_bridge`, `symmetric_group_not_solvable`, `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`) are wrappers composing Mathlib's `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`, `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable`, and `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`. The heart of the argument — `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` — is a 2-line `intro`/`exact` contrapositive.

This entry anchors a rich cluster of related gallery proofs: the complete solvability classification $S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$ (`abel-ruffini-galois-extensions`), the full bidirectional Galois criterion (`abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-03`), a concrete unsolvable quintic $x^5 - 4x + 2$ with $\text{Gal} \cong S_5$ (`abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01`), and the Bring-Jerrard reduction showing the quintic's 'beyond-radicals' solution via the Bring radical (`abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-07`). Together they build a complete formal picture of polynomial solvability from foundations to frontier.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: Galois theory has far-reaching consequences:

1. CONSTRUCTIBILITY: Similar techniques prove that angle trisection and cube doubling are impossible with compass and straightedge — both reduce to showing that the relevant Galois group is not a 2-group.

2. INVERSE GALOIS PROBLEM: Which groups appear as Galois groups over $\mathbb{Q}$? This remains open for many groups. Shafarevich proved every solvable group is a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$, but the general case is wide open.
openQuestions: **[Partially addressed in `inverse-galois-d4`] Constructive direction of the Galois bridge**: `galois_bridge` proves the forward implication — solvability by radicals implies solvable Galois group — and the proof uses this direction contrapositively.

**[Addressed in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-02`]** Mathlib instances for $S_2, S_3, S_4$ were missing at time of writing — `IsSolvable` instances stopped at the general 'abelian groups are solvable' lemma and the negative result `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` for $n \geq 5$, leaving the explicit positive cases as a typeclass gap.

**[Partially addressed in `inverse-galois-oq-02`, `abel-ruffini-galois-extensions-oq-05`, and `abel-ruffini-galois-extensions-oq-05-oq-01`]** The Inverse Galois Problem — whether every finite group appears as a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$ — is a deep open problem.

**[Partially addressed in `abel-ruffini-oq-04`]** The file relies on `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` and `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` as black boxes. The sub-entry `abel-ruffini-oq-04` exposes the internal proof chain from $A_5$ simplicity through the derived series to the Abel-Ruffini impossibility as individually named pedagogical theorems.

**[Partially addressed in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-07`]** Charles Hermite (1858) showed that the general quintic *can* be solved using elliptic modular functions — bypassing the radical barrier by expanding the class of allowed operations.

In positive characteristic $p > 0$, the Abel-Ruffini picture changes dramatically: the Abhyankar conjecture (proved by Raynaud 1994, Harbater 1994) characterizes which finite groups occur as Galois groups of covers of $\mathbb{A}^1$ over algebraically closed fields of characteristic $p$ — every group whose $p$-Sylow subgroup is a $p$-group appears.
**Galois group computation and the resolvent method**: `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` requires exhibiting a polynomial with non-solvable Galois group to give a concrete unsolvable quintic.

**Arnold-Khovanskii topological proof**: Can Arnold's topological proof of Abel-Ruffini (using monodromy groups of algebraic functions and the fundamental group of $\mathbb{C}^5 \setminus \Delta$ where $\Delta$ is the discriminant locus) be formalized in Lean 4?

**[Partially addressed in `abel-ruffini-oq-09`] Differential Galois theory and Liouville's theorem on integration**: The direct analog of Abel-Ruffini for integration — Liouville's theorem (1835) that $\int e^{-x^2} dx$ cannot be expressed in elementary functions — is proved via differential Galois theory (Picard-Vessiot theory).

**[Partially addressed in `abel-ruffini-oq-10`] Chebotarev density in Lean**: Chebotarev's density theorem (1922) is the engine of computational Galois theory — the cycle-type distribution of Frobenius elements over primes equals the cycle-type distribution of group elements.

mainTheorems.name: not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal
mainTheorems.description: **Abel-Ruffini in contrapositive form** — the central theorem of the file and the modern statement of the 1824 impossibility result.
mainTheorems.leanType: (α : E) → (q : Polynomial F) → Irreducible q → aeval α q = 0 → ¬ IsSolvable q.Gal → ¬ IsSolvableByRad F α

mainTheorems.name: galois_bridge
mainTheorems.description: **The Galois Bridge** — the structural pivot of the entire formalization, a pure wrapper around Mathlib's `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` (in `Mathlib.FieldTheory.AbelRuffini`) that renames it for pedagogical clarity.
mainTheorems.leanType: (α : E) → (q : Polynomial F) → Irreducible q → aeval α q = 0 → IsSolvableByRad F α → IsSolvable q.Gal

mainTheorems.name: symmetric_group_not_solvable
mainTheorems.description: **The group-theoretic heart of Abel-Ruffini** — the unsolvability of $S_n$ for $n \geq 5$, stated for the canonical Lean type $\mathrm{Equiv.Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)$.

mainTheorems.name: s5_not_solvable
mainTheorems.description: **The classical Abel-Ruffini obstruction at $n = 5$** — the unique specialization of `symmetric_group_not_solvable` that mathematicians from 1824 onward had in mind when they said "the quintic is unsolvable".

mainTheorems.name: s6_not_solvable
mainTheorems.description: **The Abel-Ruffini obstruction at $n = 6$** — the smallest non-special-case extension of `s5_not_solvable`, illustrating the pattern $\forall n \geq 5,\, S_n$ not solvable.

mainTheorems.name: a5_is_simple
mainTheorems.description: **The mathematical keystone of Abel-Ruffini** — the simplicity of $A_5$, formalized as Mathlib's `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`. Statement: `IsSimpleGroup (alternatingGroup (Fin 5))`, meaning $A_5$ has no nontrivial proper normal subgroups.

mainTheorems.name: s0_solvable
mainTheorems.description: **Boundary of the solvability spectrum, lower end** — $S_0 = \mathrm{Equiv.Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,0)$, the permutation group of the empty type, is the trivial group $\{e\}$, hence solvable.

mainTheorems.name: s1_solvable
mainTheorems.description: **Boundary of the solvability spectrum, lower end (continued)** — $S_1 = \mathrm{Equiv.Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,1)$, the permutation group of a one-element type, is again the trivial group $\{e\}$, hence solvable.

mainTheorems.name: exists_quintic
mainTheorems.description: **Placeholder existence statement** — proves that *some* degree-5 polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$ exists, with the trivial witness $X^5$.
